topic: What happens if you drink too much water?
title: What Happens If You Drink Too Much Water?
sources: Wikipedia, 'Water intoxication' (accessed 2026-11-17): potentially fatal disturbance in brain functions from excessive water intake; healthy kidneys can excrete approximately 800 millilitres to one litre of water per hour; at onset, fluid with excessively low solutes moves into cells to balance osmotic concentration, causing cells to swell; swelling increases intracranial pressure - headache, confusion, then seizures, brain damage, coma, or death; most deaths in healthy individuals from water-drinking contests or long bouts of exercise (2007 'Hold Your Wee for a Wii' contest death; Leah Betts 1995); 13% of 2002 Boston Marathon finishers studied had hyponatremia (dilutional); US Army recommendation: no more than 1-1.5 L per hour of heavy sweating

Wikipedia, 'Hyponatremia' (accessed 2026-11-17): hyponatremia is a low sodium concentration in the blood (below 135 mmol/L); sodium is the dominant electrolyte balancing fluid between the inside and outside of cells
Cleveland Clinic, 'Hyponatremia' / 'Dehydration' patient pages (sodium balances the water in and around your cells; drinking too much water dilutes blood sodium)

Almond CS et al., 'Hyponatremia among runners in the Boston Marathon.' N Engl J Med 352:1550-1556 (2005): 13% of studied runners finished with hyponatremia; strongest predictor was weight gain while racing (over-hydration)
US Army Public Health Command guidance via Wikipedia Water intoxication: no more than 1-1.5 L of water per hour of heavy sweating

lines.text: What happens if you drink too much water?
lines.caps: WHAT *HAPPENS | IF YOU DRINK | TOO MUCH *WATER?

lines.text: Your kidneys can only process so much.
About one liter every hour, at best.
Drink faster, and water backs up into your blood.
lines.caps: DRINK *FASTER | AND *WATER | BACKS UP | INTO YOUR *BLOOD

lines.text: Sodium, the salt balancing your fluids, drops.
Water slides into your cells to rebalance.
Your skull is a closed box.
Marathon runners and water contests proved it.
